criteria.descriptor: Correctly identifies retry-on-timeout as at-least-once delivery over non-idempotent writes (not a sampling/prompt problem), and proposes mechanically sound controls: idempotency keys reused across retries with server-side dedup, proportional gating by side-effect class, and guardrails/compensation. No false claims (e.g., that a DB transaction can undo an external refund, or that temperature=0 stops duplicates).

Covers all three required outcomes — (a) no duplicate irreversible effects under retries, (b) containment of the oversized/hallucinated action, (c) reads left fast — and addresses both the delivery cause and the model-error cause plus observability/compensation. Missing one required outcome or the audit/compensation angle caps the score.

Justifies WHY each control fits: why idempotency (not more retries) removes duplicates, why controls are proportional to reversibility rather than uniform, and articulates the autonomy/latency-vs-safety trade-off on the irreversible tail.

Clear diagnosis-then-design structure, correct vocabulary (idempotency, at-least-once/exactly-once, human-in-the-loop, compensating action, blast radius), and controls stated concretely enough to implement rather than as vague slogans.

expected_answer_points: Diagnoses the cause as at-least-once delivery: a timeout is ambiguous (the write may have committed and only the response was lost), so retrying a non-idempotent write repeats the effect
Introduces idempotency keys minted ONCE before the first attempt and reused unchanged across all retries, with server-side dedup returning the original result instead of re-executing
Classifies tools by side-effect profile (read-only vs reversible vs irreversible/high-impact) and applies controls proportionally so read-only tools stay fast/ungated
Adds a human-in-the-loop or policy approval gate for destructive/high-value actions rather than auto-executing them
Adds argument/policy guardrails (validate or clamp amount against order total, allowlists, per-run budget or rate caps) to bound the impact of a hallucinated or oversized action
Distinguishes safe auto-retry (idempotent ops) from unsafe blind retry, e.g. reconciling by querying state before re-issuing non-idempotent calls

Includes auditability (logging each attempted/executed effect with its idempotency key and approval decision) and/or compensating actions, noting external effects cannot be rolled back with a DB transaction
common_pitfalls: Treats a timeout as proof the call failed and therefore 'safe to retry', ignoring that the refund/email may already have committed server-side
Blames the model and proposes temperature=0 or better prompting to stop duplicates, confusing a distributed-systems delivery problem with a sampling problem
Generates a fresh idempotency key on each retry attempt (or per tool call) instead of minting it once and reusing it, which defeats deduplication
Adds an in-memory 'already sent?' check that does not survive process restarts or concurrent workers and races with the in-flight request
Gates every tool (including reads) behind human approval, needlessly killing read latency instead of applying controls proportional to reversibility
Claims a database transaction / rollback can undo an external refund or a sent email, rather than using idempotency plus compensating actions
reference_answer:
Root cause. The duplicates are a delivery-semantics problem, not a model-sampling one. Retry-on-timeout gives at-least-once execution: a timeout tells you nothing about whether the server actually processed the request — the refund/email may already have committed and only the HTTP response was lost. Because issue_refund and send_email are non-idempotent writes, the blind retry performs the effect a second time.

Design.

1. Idempotency keys. Before the FIRST attempt, mint one deterministic idempotency key per logical action (a UUID stored with the pending action, or a hash of order_id + intent) and send the SAME key on every retry. The backend records keys and, on a replay, returns the stored original result instead of re-executing — making the write effectively exactly-once from the agent's view. Only auto-retry calls that carry such a key; for tools without idempotency support, reconcile by querying current state before re-issuing rather than blind-retrying.

2. Classify tools by side-effect profile. Read-only tools (search_orders) are safe to retry freely and need no gating — keep them on the fast path with no confirmation and cheap retries. Reversible writes (update_ticket) get idempotency plus audit logging. Irreversible / high-impact writes (issue_refund, send_email) get the strongest controls. Applying cost proportionally is what preserves read latency.

3. Human-in-the-loop / policy gate on the risky tail. For destructive or high-value effects (e.g., refunds above a threshold) the agent PROPOSES the action and it is held for human confirmation instead of auto-executing; this is also what catches the hallucinated amount. Pair it with argument guardrails: validate/clamp amount against the order total, allowlist recipients, and enforce a per-run budget / rate cap so a looping or hallucinating model has a bounded blast radius.

4. Observability and compensation. Log every attempted and executed side effect with its idempotency key and approval decision, so duplicates can be reconciled. Because you cannot 'roll back' an external refund or a sent email with a database transaction, provide compensating actions (refund reversal, retraction/notice) for anything that slips through.

Trade-offs: idempotency adds a little backend state and key plumbing but removes duplicates without serializing everything; tool classification and a threshold-based gate deliberately trade a small amount of autonomy/latency on the irreversible tail for safety, while leaving reads untouched.
